teaching.causalExplanation: Start with the travel times. A cluster is a group of values bunched close together. There are two here. One from six to eighteen minutes, and one from forty-two to fifty-five. A gap is a stretch of the number line with no values at all, here from eighteen to forty-two minutes. The syllabus asks you to explain them, in context. The short times are students who walk, ride or get dropped off. The long ones are bus students, because the bus winds through other suburbs first. Nobody takes about half an hour, because students either make a short trip on foot, by bike or by car, or ride the long bus route. There's nothing in between. Two clusters usually mean two groups mixed together, like the bimodal shapes from before. Then the lone value, ninety-five minutes. An outlier is a value well away from the rest of the data. It needs an explanation too. Maybe the bus broke down that day, or the student missed it and waited for the next one. Our sleep data's three hour night looks like an outlier as well, two and a half hours below the next shortest night. Maybe that student flew home late from a trip, or was sick. But looks can fool you. How far away is far enough? We need a fair test, the same for every dataset, so different people reach the same answer. Here's the test, built from the box. Take the IQR, the width of the middle half, and multiply it by one and a half. Then step that far out from each quartile. Those cut-offs are called fences. For our sleep, Q one is six and a half, Q three is eight, and the IQR is one and a half. One and a half times one and a half is two point two five. The lower fence is six and a half minus two point two five, four point two five. The upper fence is eight plus two point two five, ten point two five. Any value below the lower fence, or above the upper fence, is an outlier. The three hour night is below four point two five, so it's an outlier. Five and a half isn't, and nothing reaches ten point two five. A common slip is subtracting just one and a half. It's one and a half times the IQR.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's the test, built from the box. Take the IQR, the width of the middle half, and multiply it by one and a half. Then step that far out from each quartile. Those cut-offs are called fences. For our sleep, Q one is six and a half, Q three is eight, and the IQR is one and a half. One and a half times one and a half is two point two five. The lower fence is six and a half minus two point two five, four point two five. The upper fence is eight plus two point two five, ten point two five. Any value below the lower fence, or above the upper fence, is an outlier. The three hour night is below four point two five, so it's an outlier. Five and a half isn't, and nothing reaches ten point two five. A common slip is subtracting just one and a half. It's one and a half times the IQR.

scenes.teachingReason: Finding an outlier is the start, not the end. First, check the record. Did someone type three when they meant eight? If it's an error, correct it. If it's genuine, a real short night, keep it, and report it. You can describe the data with it and without it, and we'll see next time how much it changes. What you never do is delete a value just to make the data look tidy. And use your eyes as well as the rule. Run the fences on the travel times, and the upper fence is a hundred and six minutes, so the ninety-five passes. The big gap between the clusters makes the IQR wide. The rule is fair, but it works best when there's one cluster.
